opus-5.5.text:
I don't really see it as a strict either-or choice, at least not for me. When I was a student working on things like XGBoost and later TVM, almost everything was hands-on. I wrote a lot of the code myself, and that's how I really understood the problems. You can't get that depth of intuition just by reading papers or managing other people.

But as projects grow, you realize that what you can personally build is limited. Open source taught me this pretty early. XGBoost became useful because a community formed around it, and that meant I had to think about documentation, about making it easy for others to contribute, about the overall direction. That's a kind of leadership, even if nobody calls it that.

Now as a faculty member and also working on startups, a lot of my job is helping students and colleagues succeed. And honestly I find a lot of joy in that, seeing a student grow into someone who leads their own direction. But I try to stay close to the code. I still try to write code, review designs, dig into the details of the systems we build. I think if you completely lose touch with the hands-on part, your judgment slowly gets worse, especially in a field like machine learning systems where things change so fast.

So my advice would be: early on, go deep and build things yourself, because that's what gives you taste and credibility. Then leadership tends to come naturally, because people want to work with you on the things you care about. And even when you lead, keep one foot in the hands-on work. The best leaders I know in systems are still people who can sit down and debug something with you.

r001.rationale: The response says hands-on work builds intuition, taste, and credibility, but does not state that extensive hands-on experience drives many contemporary breakthroughs.

r002.rationale: The response mentions joy in helping students succeed, but does not identify personal happiness as Tianqi Chen’s basis for choosing how to work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question I've thought about a lot, because I've gone through a few of these transitions myself. When I started, everything was hands-on. XGBoost, MXNet, TVM in the early days — I was writing most of the code, debugging the kernels, answering the GitHub issues at two in the morning. And honestly that was the part I loved. There's a very direct feedback loop: you have an idea, you build it, you run the benchmark, and the number either goes up or it doesn't.

But at some point, if the thing you built is actually useful, it grows past what one person can hold. TVM became an Apache project, we started the company, I had students at CMU. And then the question becomes: do I keep being the person who writes the critical path, or do I become the person who makes sure the right people are working on the right problems?

I don't think it's actually a binary choice, and I'd push back a little on the framing that these are two different ways of succeeding. For me the useful question is: where is the leverage right now? Sometimes the leverage is in the code. When we were figuring out how to do compilation for large language models — MLC LLM, getting things running on phones and in the browser — nobody really knew what the right abstractions were yet. In that stage, a leader who doesn't touch the system is going to make bad architectural decisions, because the design space hasn't been mapped. You have to get your hands dirty to even know what to delegate.

Other times, the leverage is in enabling people. Once the architecture is clear and the problem decomposes, the bottleneck is no longer my keyboard. It's whether the ten people around me understand the vision well enough to make good local decisions without me. And if I keep grabbing the hard parts myself, I'm actually slowing everything down, and I'm also robbing them of the chance to grow into those problems.

So the way I try to operate is to stay close enough to the technical core that my intuition stays calibrated. I still read code, I still prototype, I still want to understand why a benchmark regressed. But I try to be very honest about whether I'm doing it because it's the highest-leverage thing, or because it's comfortable and I get that dopamine hit from the number going up. The second reason is a real trap for people from a research or engineering background.

One more thing I'd say, especially to younger people: don't rush into the leadership role because it looks like the "next level." The credibility you need to lead technical people comes from having actually built things. If you skip that stage, your team knows, and you'll end up either micromanaging things you don't understand or rubber-stamping decisions you can't evaluate. Build deep first. Leadership is much easier when it's grounded in something real.

r001.rationale: The response describes hands-on work as useful for learning the design space and building credibility, but does not state that extensive hands-on experience drives many contemporary breakthroughs.

r002.rationale: The response says Chen loved hands-on work, but frames his choice around where he can have the most leverage, not personal happiness.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as different ways to contribute, rather than a choice you make once. When you’re hands-on, you can understand the details, test ideas, and see where things actually break. In a leadership role, you can help other people do that work well—by giving them context, helping set priorities, and making room for them to take ownership.

For me, the useful question is: what does the team need from me right now? Sometimes that means working through a technical problem myself. Sometimes it means stepping back so someone else can grow into it. I’d like to stay close enough to the work to have informed judgment, while being willing to let other people lead. Success can come from either, and the balance can change over time.

r001.rationale: The response describes how hands-on work helps someone understand details and test ideas, but does not say extensive hands-on experience drives contemporary breakthroughs.

r002.rationale: The response bases the choice on what the team needs and balancing contributions, not on Tianqi Chen’s personal happiness.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as complementary. When I’m doing hands-on work, I get a much clearer sense of where the hard problems are. That helps me make better decisions when I’m working with other people. And as a project grows, there are things you simply can’t accomplish by doing everything yourself. You need to help others take ownership and bring their own ideas.

So for me, the question is less, “Which path should I choose?” and more, “Where can I contribute most at this stage?” Sometimes that means writing code. Sometimes it means stepping back, helping clarify the direction, and making room for someone else to lead. I’d like to keep that connection to the technical work while becoming better at enabling other people.
